title: Coroner Finds Melbourne Girl's Hospital Death From Myocarditis Was Preventable
excerpt: Victoria's deputy state coroner found earlier escalation after an abnormal ECG could have saved eight-year-old Amrita Lanka, who died at Monash Medical Centre in 2022.
body:
• Victoria's deputy state coroner found that the 2022 death of eight-year-old Amrita Varshini Lanka from lymphocytic myocarditis at Monash Medical Centre was preventable.
  • An abnormal ECG at 3.30 a.m. led a registrar to suspect myocarditis, but the coroner found the severity was not appreciated and care was not escalated in time.
  • The coroner said that by about 4 a.m., once the ECG and elevated lactate results were available, Amrita's life could have been saved.
  • Monash Health had already admitted failing to appreciate the seriousness of her condition and has changed escalation rules, including notifying on-call consultants in specific cases.

An eight-year-old girl who arrived at a Melbourne hospital with stomach pain, nausea and vomiting died less than a day later from inflammation of the heart muscle — a death that should not have happened, a Victorian coroner has found.

Amrita Varshini Lanka died from lymphocytic myocarditis in the paediatric emergency department of Monash Medical Centre on April 30, 2022. On Wednesday, Deputy State Coroner Paresa Spanos handed down findings that her death was preventable, as her parents, Chandra Sekhar Lanka and Satya Tarapureddi, listened in court, according to Australian Associated Press.

The night her condition deteriorated

Amrita presented to the emergency department at about 1 p.m. on April 29, after two days of stomach pain, nausea and vomiting. Tests quickly ruled out appendicitis, and staff began treating her on the basis that she had gastroenteritis.

Early the next morning, her mother raised concerns that Amrita had chest pain and shortness of breath. An electrocardiogram at 3.30 a.m. came back abnormal and led emergency registrar Patrick Tan to suspect myocarditis. He consulted a colleague, who agreed with that preliminary view.

But neither doctor appreciated the severity of her condition, the coroner found. Her blood pressure was not measured at that time, while other testing showed elevated lactate, a sign she was deteriorating. Reporting by Times Now World on the inquest said Tan was 12 weeks into his first paediatric rotation and overseeing about 18 patients, and that a later troponin result was far above the normal threshold.

"Amrita's life could have been saved."

— Paresa Spanos, Victoria Deputy State Coroner

Spanos said that certainly by about 4 a.m., when the ECG had been completed and the elevated lactate was available, earlier escalation and transfer to the Royal Children's Hospital could have saved her.

Escalation came too late

Despite the abnormal ECG, Tan judged that Amrita did not look unwell and did not attend to her again until 5.30 a.m., when her condition had clearly worsened, AAP reported. Her care was then escalated to senior clinicians and specialist units, but she suffered a brief cardiac arrest at 7.30 a.m.

Staff organised an emergency transfer to the Royal Children's Hospital. A crew arrived at about 8.51 a.m., by which time Amrita had gone into prolonged cardiac arrest. CPR could not save her.

Spanos accepted that emergency departments are busy and that Tan was a relatively junior doctor with many responsibilities. She still found that the clinical management and care he provided was wanting and that it caused or contributed to Amrita's death.

What the hospital has changed

At a 2024 inquest, Monash Health admitted staff had failed to appreciate the seriousness of Amrita's condition. The coroner made no formal recommendations. Instead, she commended Monash Health for an internal review after the death and noted a series of changes it had implemented, including requiring emergency clinicians to notify on-call consultants in specific cases.

For parents reading this case outside Australia, the concrete lesson in the findings is about escalation, not diagnosis at home: chest pain and breathlessness in a child who is deteriorating were the warning signs Amrita's mother raised at about 3 a.m., and the coroner's criticism focused on what clinicians did — and did not do — in the hours after those signs and an abnormal ECG were recorded.

What happens next

The findings close the coronial process without formal recommendations, leaving the changes already made by Monash Health as the institutional response. For Amrita's parents, who did not speak to media as they left court, the ruling records in official terms what they heard in the courtroom: with earlier escalation, their daughter could have lived.
